articles.title: In the city where Haitian deportees are being sent, locals say they’re not ready
articles.summary: Thursday marked the first deportation flight to Haiti from the US since the revocation of Temporary Protected Status.
articles.body: Haiti’s northern coast is where the country faces the vast Atlantic with all its baggage. There’s Labadie, the private resort open only to American cruise ships and foreign holiday makers. Just next door is Ile de la Tortue, an infamous way station for human traffickers. And then there’s Cap-Haitien, a city steeped in the country’s revolutionary history – and more recently, the first-choice destination for the Trump administration to deport Haitian migrants. Since Haiti’s devastating earthquake in 2010, Cap-Haitien has been a major hub for internally displaced people fleeing disaster and violence in other parts of the country. And after the Trump administration’s legal victory this month to remove temporary deportation protections from hundreds of thousands of people in the United States, the city may soon see many more arrivals. Thursday marked the first deportation flight to Haiti from the US since the revocation of Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which had protected about 350,000 Haitians in the US from deportation and given them legal work permits. Now Haitian communities across the US are coming to terms with the new reality that they’re vulnerable to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “It’s a great day to deport illegal aliens. Good morning America!” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted on X Thursday morning, hours before the deportation flight to Haiti took off. A little after noon, 161 people descended from the charter flight in Cap-Haitien, according to Haiti’s National Migration Office. Some fell to their knees to kiss the ground, others covered their faces and hurried away from the gathered local press. The question in Cap is how many more will follow. Locals say the city is already inundated. “Cap-Haitian alone can’t receive more people,” said Demonstène Reynold, a mechanic living in Cap. “We’re not just receiving deportees from outside of Haiti … due to the political crisis, we have people from Hinche and Port-au-Prince, from the interior of the country.” The city these days looks different from years past. Street traffic is snarled, trash collection sites overflow. A hospital visited by CNN was overwhelmed with patients queuing outdoors, mothers rocking babies in the heat as they waited. Louis Ronald Espoir, an administrator at the city’s Hospital Fort Saint Michel, said the city’s medical facilities are at capacity. “As you can see here with your own eyes, all the hospitals in the region are full despite the best efforts of the government. If they’re full with the current population, I’d be lying to say we can take in anyone else.” Thursday’s flight comes as immigrant rights advocates in the US raise concerns about the dangers of deporting people to the Caribbean nation. Critics, who want more immigration restrictions, have accused the Trump administration of not removing undocumented immigrants quickly enough. The Trump administration has repeatedly argued that Haiti is safe enough for Haitians to be returned to, despite a State Department “Do not travel” advisory and a Federal Aviation Administration ban on US commercial flights there. In a June interview on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Mullin defended the decision to send Haitians back and argued that the country would benefit from the returnees. The State Department’s “do not travel” advisory was issued out of concern for Americans, not Haitians, he said, “because they are kidnapping or trying to kidnap individuals from the United States because they feel like they – their family has the money to pay the ransom.” But the country’s kidnapping epidemic has been overwhelmingly felt by Haitians, with gangs notorious for taking victims from among even the very poor. The brutal business is centered around capital Port-au-Prince, where US deportation flights have also landed. CNN is seeking comment from DHS about Thursday’s flight to Cap-Haitien, why the passengers onboard were deported and whether any of them are among those who recently lost TPS. On the far side of the country from Port-au-Prince, Cap-Haitien is considered largely safe from gang violence. But some worry a large influx of newcomers could destabilize an already crowded place. Angie Bell, the city’s former mayor, says she encourages people to come back – but that the country needs to build its ability to welcome them. “We need much more development, and we need more security as a preventative measure, with so many people coming in,” Bell says. She estimates that the city’s population has shot up from around 350,000 people in the last census in 2003, to at least 800,000. “Because of the lack of housing, we have a lot of people that are working in the city but living in the outskirts,” she said. The Haitian government and aid organizations like the International Office for Migration are working to ease the burden on locals and help new arrivals disperse across the country. Deportees are typically offered food and some money for their onward travel, as well as a place to stay for a few nights and assistance in locating family members. But as the population numbers suggest, many are not moving on from Cap-Haitien. And not all the deportees will even know where to go. According to the head of Haiti’s migration agency, Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, who met Thursday’s deportation flight at the airport, one of the disembarking passengers had never been to Haiti before. Born in the Dominican Republic to Haitian parents before moving to the US, it was unclear where he should go next, Delva said, adding, “he knows nothing of Haiti.” Reporting contributed by CNN’s Catherine Shoichet.

articles.title: Big crisis brewing in Rawalpindi? Pakistan deploys army for âsensitive dutiesâ
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for.
articles.body: The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".Army deployment follows security incidentThe decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi. He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.Rawalpindi has strategic importanceThe deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Hindu family of four found dead in locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur; strangulation suspected
articles.summary: South Asia News: Four members of a Hindu family, including a retired schoolteacher, were found dead inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city under suspici.
articles.body: Four members of a Hindu family, including a retired schoolteacher, were found dead inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city under suspicious circumstances, with police investigation under way, as per ANI citing local media.The bodies of Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata, 50, their daughter Agami, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area around 11.30pm on Saturday, police said, suspecting strangulation and robbery in inital probe.The bodies were found in different parts of the house. Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof, those of his wife and daughter from the staircase, and Priyamâs body from under a bed, according to Subir Chowdhury, in-charge of Rangpur Metropolitan CID.âThe household belongings were found scattered and in disarray. For now, it appears to be a robbery. However, nothing can be confirmed until the investigation is completed,â Chowdhury said, as quoted by Bangladesh local The Daily Star.Meanwhile, Sanatan Chakrabarty, deputy commissioner of Rangpur Metropolitan Police and head of the Detective Branch, said the victims were initially suspected to have been strangled. The bodies were sent to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for autopsies, while police, CID and Detective Branch teams launched a joint investigation.The family had not been heard from since Thursday. Pritilataâs sister Puja Chakraborty told The Daily Star that all four phones had been switched off since Thursday night.âWe came to Daspara on Saturday night after finding their phones switched off. The main gate of the house was locked and all the lights inside were off. Police later arrived, broke the lock and entered the house, where they recovered the bodies,â she said.Ganapati had retired from Rangpur Zilla School in December last year and had since been working as a homeopathic practitioner. His daughter had completed a masterâs degree in English, while his son was a Class 5 student.The family had lived in the area for about four years and Ganapati had built the three-storey house, although construction was still incomplete, locals said.Rangpur police commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said the investigation was being treated as a priority. âWe will know how they died once we receive the autopsy reports,â he said.The deaths come amid continued concern over attacks and violence involving Bangladeshâs Hindu minority. Human Rights Watch has reported attacks on Hindu homes, while minority groups have documented a broader pattern of violence against religious minorities. However, there is currently no evidence as of now establishing that the Rangpur killings were communal or linked to the victimsâ religion.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pasta factory expansion leads to stunning discovery of 2,600-year-old city of the dead
articles.summary: Pasta Garofalo's factory expansion in Gragnano uncovered burial chambers with grave goods connecting Greek, Egyptian and Etruscan civilizations.
articles.body: A pasta factory expansion in Italy took an unexpected turn when archaeologists uncovered a 2,600-year-old city of the dead, filled with ancient tombs and rare treasures. The necropolis was found at the Pasta Garofalo factory in Gragnano, a town near Naples, according to a news release issued by the company. The excavation was conducted between 2025 and 2026 ahead of an expansion of Pasta Garofalo's production facility, with the findings recently announced by the company in July. 2,000-YEAR-OLD ROMAN RECIPES BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE — HERE'S WHAT THEY ACTUALLY TASTE LIKE The site, which dates to the first half of the sixth century B.C., was built during the Archaic period of Mediterranean history, centuries before the rise of the Roman Empire. Pictures from the excavation show rows of stone burial chambers at the site, along with human remains, pottery and other artifacts. Several burial chambers contained rarely preserved materials, including textiles, wooden objects and woven baskets, which officials said "deepen[s] understanding of funerary practices, social organization and everyday life during the Archaic period." Officials also reported that the grave goods found at the site were "remarkable" and included Egyptian scarabs, animal-shaped amber ornaments and "silver and bronze artifacts of Etruscan origin." ARCHAEOLOGISTS REVEAL NUTRITIOUS FOOD REMAINS DISCOVERED IN ANCIENT VILLA QUARTERS "These exceptional finds testify to the central role played by the ancient territory of Gragnano within Mediterranean trade networks, serving as a crossroads connecting the Greek, Egyptian and Etruscan worlds," the statement read. The discovery held special significance for Pasta Garofalo, the company said, given its centuries-old ties to Gragnano and its pasta-making tradition. Pasta Garofalo "has celebrated the deep bond between pasta and the town of Gragnano ... [and] this relationship has been further enriched by an extraordinary new chapter," according to the release. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Massimo Menna, chief executive officer of Pasta Garofalo, said the discovery "fills us with great pride and a profound sense of responsibility." "Our history is inseparably linked to Gragnano, a place that has safeguarded a unique heritage of culture, tradition and manufacturing expertise for centuries," Menna said. "We believe that doing business also means caring for the places where we operate, contributing to their knowledge and enhancement." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Researchers will continue studying the human remains to learn more about the ancient community's diet, movements and living conditions. "Ongoing research will prioritize the analysis of the osteological remains to examine diets, mobility patterns and living conditions of the communities that occupied the region during the Archaic period," the statement noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The discovery follows other significant necropolis-related finds across Italy in recent years. Earlier this year, officials found the remains of an ancient sanctuary in northern Italy after construction crews unexpectedly uncovered the site while working on a new highway. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In 2025, archaeologists discovered a nearly 3,000-year-old "city of the dead" in Trento, Italy, dating back to the Iron Age.

Officials also reported that the grave goods found at the site were "remarkable" and included Egyptian scarabs, animal-shaped amber ornaments and "silver and bronze artifacts of Etruscan origin." The discovery held special significance for Pasta Garofalo, the company said, given its centuries-old ties to Gragnano and its pasta-making tradition. Pasta Garofalo "has celebrated the deep bond between pasta and the town of Gragnano ... [and] this relationship has been further enriched by an extraordinary new chapter," according to the release. "Our history is inseparably linked to Gragnano, a place that has safeguarded a unique heritage of culture, tradition and manufacturing expertise for centuries," Menna said. "We believe that doing business also means caring for the places where we operate, contributing to their knowledge and enhancement." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Researchers will continue studying the human remains to learn more about the ancient community's diet, movements and living conditions. "Ongoing research will prioritize the analysis of the osteological remains to examine diets, mobility patterns and living conditions of the communities that occupied the region during the Archaic period," the statement noted. articles.title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
articles.summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
articles.body: Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him. Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor. The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again. MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027. "Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X. Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government. He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions. Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents. MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED "I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote. Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum. Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open. 5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X. "No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote. "Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added. U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States. Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The case has strained relations between the U.S. and Mexico. Sheinbaum has called the charges foreign interference, while Mexico says Washington has not provided enough evidence to justify Rocha’s arrest or extradition.

articles.title: Service resumes on CrossCountry trains after power outage
articles.summary: It follows major national rail disruption at the weekend.
articles.body:
Train operator CrossCountry says it expects to run a full service on Monday after cancelling nearly all of its UK services the day before following a power cut at its control centre.

The outage in Birmingham at the weekend brought disruption from Glasgow to Penzance.

Major routes were affected between Birmingham and Manchester, which pass through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton. Journeys from Leeds to York and Cheltenham to Cardiff were also caught in the travel chaos, leaving passengers frustrated.

On Monday morning, CrossCountry reported a handful of service cancellations, although these were put down to trains departing late and staff shortages.

Customers are advised to check their journey before travelling.

The operator on Sunday thanked passengers for their patience and understanding during the disruption.

Tickets purchased for travel on CrossCountry services on Sunday will be valid for travel on CrossCountry services until Wednesday, the company has said.

On Sunday, a range of personal experiences were shared by passengers.

Andy Burton, from Worcester, was travelling back from Cromford to Worcester after spending the weekend away with family celebrating his sister's birthday, but only got as far as Derby before his journey came to a premature end.

He was forced to stay the night in a budget hotel in the hope he could return home on Monday.

"It was only once I had arrived at Derby that a member of staff told me my planned alternative route via Leicester had also been cancelled, because it was part of the CrossCountry disruption," he said.

"I soon realised I was stranded, as they said there was no alternative train route back to Worcester.

"It's not the best end to a great weekend away."

Reese Proctor described the cancellations as "frustrating and unacceptable" as he tried to get to Manchester's Etihad Stadium in time for a 14:00 BST kick-off against Bournemouth.

He had hoped to get a train from Reading to Manchester, but instead resorted to driving more than 100 miles to his friend's house in Leicester before driving on to the stadium.

The 22-year-old told BBC Newsbeat the drive had added an extra two hours to his journey, leaving him "fuming".

A number of services resumed on Sunday evening, including an hourly train service from Birmingham New Street to Leicester and Derby.

On Sunday, Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "concerned" by the situation.

She said: "We are setting up Great British Railways and nationalising services, including CrossCountry next year, to end decades of fragmentation and vulnerability on our network. We are determined to give passengers the reliability they deserve."

The National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT) has called for a review of railway operational control centres following the disruption, "to ensure they remain unaffected by power outages".

RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said passengers and rail workers should not have to face another week of "travel chaos" because of unreliable back-up systems.

CrossCountry was ranked Britain's worst rail operator in June.

Have you been affected by the disruption?

articles.title: Father of sailor aboard the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln detained by immigration authorities, family says
articles.summary: Joshua Aviles said he has been “fighting for a country that has given me everything,” only to learn his father had been detained.
articles.body: The immigrant father of a sailor on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln was anxiously awaiting his son’s return home when immigration authorities detained him over the weekend. Luis Manuel Aviles was taken into custody late Saturday morning near a Publix supermarket in Key West, Florida, where he lives, as he was headed to a mechanic, according to three family members. “He was excited because he was finally going to be able to hug his son,” his wife, who requested her name not be published, told Noticias Telemundo on Sunday. A Navy official confirmed to NBC News on Monday that their son, Joshua Aviles, who is a handling airman, is currently assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln. The 25-year-old has been deployed inside the aircraft carrier for nine months, which is considered a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea. Aviles’ wife said the father “was very happy, counting the days and weeks until his son arrived so he could hug him. And then, this happened.” Originally from Nicaragua, Aviles has been living in the U.S. for 20 years, mostly working as a handyman for hotels in Key West alongside a string of other jobs to provide for his family, according to his youngest son, Luisito Aviles, and stepdaughter, Katty Delgado. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Sunday that Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles during a traffic stop in Key West. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings. “We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said. In an interview with Noticias Telemundo on Sunday, Luisito Aviles described his father as the person who’s taught him everything he knows, from electrical issues to how to be a strong person. “He never hid, he always did things the right way,” Luisito Aviles said in Spanish, adding that his father was working toward getting legal status and had complied with his paperwork and visits to ICE’s offices. Delgado told NBC News on Saturday evening that she has no knowledge of an arrest history or criminal allegations against Luis Manuel Aviles. “He’s doing everything the right way,” she said. Delgado said that she learned the news from family members, including Aviles’ wife and his son Joshua Aviles, who posted a note about the detention on Facebook. Joshua Aviles wrote on Facebook on Saturday, “I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything.” He said that his father is hard-working, giving and humble and that he has a work permit, a Social Security card and a driver’s license. “This is heartbreaking for me,” Joshua Aviles said. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.” Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS told NBC News and Telemundo, NBCUniversal’s Spanish-language network, that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.” The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego on Nov. 25, and, with more than eight months since it visited a port in December, it broke the Navy record for time without a port call. Relatives of sailors on board the carrier have described reports of deteriorating conditions and morale. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about the situation on board have been “completely misrepresented.” The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln has officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more. Joshua Aviles, who told NBC News he has limited internet access, wrote on Facebook that he’s doing everything he can to get his father released from detention. “I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad,” he wrote. President Donald Trump has stood by his administration’s immigration crackdown, including ICE’s expanded enforcement and arrests, which in recent months have included the arrests of children and spouses of service members, a San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator and a grandmother from India who’s a schoolteacher with a green card. Immigration authorities have detained more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during Trump’s second term, according to a recent Associated Press investigation. There has been backlash to the detentions, which come despite programs for military members that can sometimes offer immediate family protection from deportation. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website says those “discretionary options” are offered on a “case-by-case basis.” It was not immediately clear whether Luis Manuel Aviles was in the program. The DHS spokesperson said in a statement Sunday that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.” “Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the spokesperson said. Delgado lamented that her stepbrother has spent nine months out at sea, without seeing his family, “and this is what his father gets.”

articles.title: Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
articles.summary: Case fatality rate climbs to nearly 48 percent in DRC, meaning almost one in two people infected with Ebola are dying.
articles.body:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 5,515 confirmed cases of infection and killed 2,642 people, with 51 new cases detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, according to the latest government figures.

The update on Sunday came as Pope Leo called for ⁠international action to help contain the epidemic, which is now the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC’s history.

list 1 of 3 How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped

list 2 of 3 DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living

list 3 of 3 Ebola continues to spread in the DRC as 16,000 vaccine doses arrive

Declared in mid-May, it is the DRC’s 17th Ebola epidemic and was designated a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization (WHO), its highest alert level, also covering neighbouring Uganda.

The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, which was the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.

According to government figures, the case fatality rate in the DRC has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to nearly 48 percent now, meaning almost one in two people infected are dying.

Contact tracing, however, has improved sharply, from 30 percent in June to more than 85 percent.

The disease has also proved deadly for those fighting it. About 160 health workers have been infected, and about 45 have died, according to the WHO.

Efforts to contain the outbreak, however, have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population and a lack of critical infrastructure.

There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo , which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks.

The WHO has pledged 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed for Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. According to the global body, early data from animal trials suggest it may offer some protection against Bundibugyo.

Some 16,250 doses of the vaccine arrived in the DRC on Friday.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and other officials said the response in the DRC needs to be scaled up two to threefold to contain the outbreak and reach every affected area.

They also called for more support and protection for front-line health workers, including protective equipment, timely payment, and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill.

Abdulsalami Nasidi, a public health consultant who helped establish the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Al Jazeera that the outbreak was “getting out of hand”.

He blamed weak infection control measures and a lack of trust between authorities and affected communities for the continued transmission.

“This is no longer just a national or regional issue; it is a global issue. If it spreads to neighbouring places with lower immunity, it will be a disaster,” Nasidi added.

The WHO currently rates the risk to the global public as low, but warns that the danger inside the DRC remains very high.

Despite the surging cases, Uganda and several health zones in DRC’s Ituri and South Kivu have interrupted transmission, which the WHO said is evidence that rapid detection, decisive leadership, and community cooperation can break the chain of transmission.

At the Vatican on Sunday, Pope Leo offered prayers for the DRC, “in light of the spread of the Ebola epidemic, which is sadly ⁠claiming many lives”.

The pontiff also called for global action to help save lives.

“I urge the international community to ⁠respond in a way that also involves local communities ⁠in prevention efforts to save ⁠as many lives as possible,” he said.

articles.title: E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
articles.summary: The settlement threatens Palestinian statehood. But it could help Israel’s PM, other far-right leaders before elections.
articles.body:
The Israeli government last week invited bids for the building of more than 1,200 units, a key step towards the construction of the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank just two months before Israel’s general election.

E1 (East 1) would link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two. Both supporters and critics agree that its construction would end the possibility of a Palestinian state.

list 1 of 4 Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence

list 2 of 4 Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan

list 3 of 4 Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement

list 4 of 4 Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage

The move has drawn international outrage, including from the United Nations.

But sections of Israel’s political class are using this global backlash to their own ends and could frame their support for E1 as a key pitch in their election campaigns.

Many on Israel’s right, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thrive on the international outrage their comments and plans draw, particularly criticism from European nations.

Since October 2023, Netanyahu has cast international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as an “us vs them” moment for the country. He has frequently framed Israel as alone in a hostile world and that he is the only leader strong enough to stand up to the country’s critics.

After the United Kingdom’s Foreign Minister Ed Miliband described E1 as an “unacceptable and destructive act”, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticised the “patronising tone” of his statement.

With the election approaching, the way ministers respond to the E1 project could determine their political futures.

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has been one of the key proponents of E1 and could benefit from an uptick in support from right-wing Israelis over the proposed illegal settlement. His Religious Zionist Party is currently unlikely to pass the electoral threshold to even run in this year’s election.

“It’s Smotrich, he’s hyping up everything under his watch ahead of the election,” Israeli analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera from Berlin, Germany.

The fact that the government’s call for tenders to construct E1 falls so close to Israel’s election is not a coincidence, Flaschenberg said. Neither is the dramatic increase in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where Smotrich has administrative control.

“Both he and even Netanyahu are benefitting from the outrage. Little of this is accidental,” the analyst added.

Condemnation of the E1 settlement has been almost universal. On Friday, the foreign ministers of Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates rejected the E1 settlement, calling for “immediate action to halt the E1 settlement plan”.

Earlier in the week, 15 European and North American leaders, including those from Israel’s traditional allies the United Kingdom, France and Germany, condemned the settlement.

In a joint letter , they said E1 would “undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank”. Some have pointed out that their failure to present any penalties if Israel goes ahead with the plan makes their criticism moot.

The United States has not criticised E1 itself, but did on Friday state its opposition to Israel’s annexation of the West Bank, which the illegal settlement could effectively result in.

“As the president has clearly stated, the US does not support Israel annexing the West Bank. A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region,” read a statement from the US Department of State.

So, is this really the end of the two-state solution?

Announcing plans for construction in August 2025, Smotrich had boasted that the new settlement would bury the “idea of a Palestinian state”.

Given that thousands of Palestinian homes have been demolished by Israel since its occupation of the West Bank began in 1967, some hope the same could happen to the illegal Israeli settlements that replaced them, if the two-state solution becomes a reality.

“The idea that this is irreversible is just nonsense. Every time there’s a new illegal settlement, voices in the West say that this is the end of the two-state solution,” Flaschenberg said.

“It definitely makes it less likely, but why the end? Every illegal settlement that’s been built can be demolished … why do we have to accept their presence as fact?”

Political analyst Ori Goldberg noted that the tender for the E1 settlement project came at a time Israel faced further international criticism for bombing an airfield in Syria and described the issuing of the tender as “a deliberate provocation”.

Thousands of Palestinians, most of them Bedouin, have already suffered home demolitions, displacement and restrictions on basic services as Israel expands its road network before construction in the occupied West Bank.

In April 2026, 23 Palestinians, including 15 children, were displaced from the az-Za’im Bedouin community following demolitions by the Israeli army.

The UN warns that the planned expansion of Israeli illegal settlements and associated infrastructure threatens to fragment the occupied West Bank and could forcibly displace the 18 Palestinian communities that have lived within the territory Israel now claims for decades.

articles.title: US threatens toughest sanctions yet against Iran: What we know
articles.summary: Tehran has threatened to retaliate against any country that joins new US economic measures.
articles.body:
With diplomacy stalled over ending the war on Iran , Washington is seeking to ratchet up pressure on Tehran with “unprecedented” economic pressure.

After United States President Donald Trump threatened to punish any country doing business with Tehran last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that a new series of economic measures will “collapse” the Iranian government, calling on countries to join the effort.

On Saturday, Tehran threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the US in economic sanctions against it.

Here’s what we know about what the US is planning and how Iran could respond.

What new measures is the US threatening against Iran?

The Trump administration has already been waging an economic pressure campaign against Iran under the banner of “Operation Economic Fury”, since the launch of the war in February.

In particular, it is currently running a naval blockade on Iranian ports in a bid to prevent oil exports and has targeted companies, brokers and tankers accused of helping Iran sell its oil abroad.

It also has longer standing sweeping sanctions in place on Iran’s oil, shipping and financial sectors, seeking to cut off the revenue Tehran earns from energy exports. It has also imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

In a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Trump announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” against Iran.

Trump said Iran had “failed to take” the opportunity to make a deal, and would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”.

He also threatened sanctions against any country that does business with Iran.

“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote.

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies – it all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are. This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”

On Thursday last week, one day after Trump’s social media tirade, Bessent told the news service CNBC that the US would apply the “toughest sanctions in history” on Iran.

“It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade [on Iran], and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” Bessent said. “It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime.”

He then offered a warning to the members of the international community that they, too, could face economic penalties if they continue to trade with Iran.

“We’re going to them and saying: You’re either with us or against us,” Bessent said. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying oil, doing seaborne ship transport – then the US Treasury and the US government, they will put its full might and force towards enforcing against you.”

He billed the US’s strategy as the “greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world”.

“It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision,” Bessent added.

Iran has decried any new, impending US sanctions – particularly economic action against other countries – as a “complete erosion of sovereignty”.

In a post on X on Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US announcement was “an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty” against the United Nations’ member states.

No state can compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports to renounce commerce with Iran, he said.

“The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism,” Baghaei said.

Iranian state media pointed out that Tehran has faced US sanctions for decades. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the new measures were “bound to fail”.

“We have seen this movie before,” Araghchi wrote on X, alongside a screenshot of a tweet from former President Barack Obama referencing earlier sanctions in 2012. “Same bull. Different bullies.”

Can Iran target countries that acquiesce to US demands?

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the IRIB state broadcaster that Iran was appealing to all countries around the world, including its neighbours, not to join the US’s “economic war”.

“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said, warning of a “seismic” retaliation.

Rezaei described Iran’s strategy as a three-stage sequence starting with talks to de-escalate tensions.

“Of course, we will first negotiate with them. We will hold talks and tell them to step aside and distance themselves from the United States. But if they do not act, we will strike. We will target that country’s interests,” he said.

Rezaei also warned Iran’s neighbours that if they participate in Trump’s economic warfare, “not even a drop of oil” will leave the Gulf region, including by alternative export routes away from the Hormuz chokepoint through which one-fifth of global oil and gas exports pass in peacetime.

Iran has already launched strikes on US military installations, infrastructure and civilian locations in the region since the war began on February 28.

Energy and other facilities in Qatar , Kuwait , Saudi Arabia , Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have also suffered damage, mostly from debris from intercepted strikes by Iran or its proxy groups across the region.

The US operates military facilities in more than a dozen locations across the Middle East and North Africa, including in Gulf nations, such as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Thousands of US soldiers are also stationed across the region, including in Jordan.

Hamidreza Azizi, a researcher on Iran at the Clingendael Institute, said in a post on X on Saturday: “Tehran appears to be trying to establish deterrence at an earlier stage, by signalling that even preparations for an attack could trigger an Iranian response.”

Azizi said two elements in the new “offensive doctrine” are emerging: preemption, which is aimed at preventing a perceived threat from materialising; and disproportionate retaliation, which is aimed at raising the cost of any attack that does occur.

How have other countries responded to Trump’s demands?

China has pushed back against Trump’s threats.

“Imposing sanctions and pressuring do not help to solve the issue,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters in Beijing on August 20.

“China calls on relevant parties to take responsible measures and solve the issues through diplomatic and political means.”

Gulf countries, which are Iran’s neighbours and also US allies, have increasingly been finding themselves caught in the middle of the war. Therefore, it is unclear if they would all join Washington in economically threatening Iran further.

Last week, the UAE, on which Iran is believed to rely for critical imports and financial services through which it sells oil, announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran, after accusing Iranian forces of firing two ballistic missiles at the country, an allegation Tehran denies.

However, analysts have told Al Jazeera that many Gulf states fear the chaos that could follow if Iran’s government were to collapse. They said that while regional confidence in diplomacy is low, no country can afford another long war.

“Ultimately, Gulf countries can’t change geography. They have to live and work alongside Iran,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera in an interview last month. “They don’t want the instability that would come from the fall of the Islamic Republic [of Iran]. I think some Gulf states have pushed for harder strikes – not to precipitate its collapse, but to weaken the more hardline elements of the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps].”

Can China and Russia insulate Iran from US measures?

While the US has made threats against any country that continues to trade with Iran, analysts say that Trump’s leverage over China and Russia , both major trading partners of Iran, is limited.

Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera last week that “it is going to be very difficult” for Trump to pull off his pressure campaign effectively.

“Trump is trying to unilaterally assert the kind of coordinated sanctions that traditionally has taken multilateral coordination, and that means getting on board China, Russia, the P5 of the UN Security Council,” Musgrave said, referring to the five permanent members of the UNSC.

This is because several sectors in Russia and China have minimal reliance on the American financial system.

Those sectors include most of China’s oil refineries . According to analytics firm Kpler, China bought 80 percent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025. Evidence of ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil off the coast of Malaysia has also shown how Iranian oil continues to be traded.

Analysts say China could also hit back if the US sanctions the major Chinese banks for processing Iranian funds, as the US Treasury has threatened .

“Trump intends to stabilise the ties with China, so [this would happen] as Beijing aims to have a temporary truce with Washington,” Yu Jie, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House think tank’s China, Asia Pacific Programme, told Al Jazeera.

Although Russia is a less significant trading partner for Iran than China, Moscow and Tehran have spent years developing critical commercial and military links designed to sidestep Western channels. Notably, Iran has provided Shahed drones to Moscow for use in its war on Ukraine.

articles.title: Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France
articles.summary: Algerian primary schools will begin teaching English before French for the first time, signalling a drift from France.
articles.body:
Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language.

English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence.

On July 25 , Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027.

French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools.

From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French.

“It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera.

It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools.

Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English.

The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets. Road signs are beginning to feature English alongside Arabic, while government ministers’ websites will also have English as an option.

The shift from French to English as Algeria’s secondary language is both sweeping and structural.

It comes amid the most serious diplomatic crisis between the two countries since Algeria’s independence from France in 1962.

In July 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron publicly backed Morocco’s sovereignty claim over Western Sahara.

Algeria, which supports the Sahrawi Polisario Front and hosts over 170,000 Sahrawi refugees, viewed that as highly provocative.

That, and other issues, saw Algeria expel French diplomats , and vice versa.

Algeria’s replacement of French as the country’s second language accelerated after the diplomatic crisis grew.

A rethink of the whole education system in Algeria may be needed.

“First and foremost, specialised training centres must be restored and candidates must not be forced into the teaching profession without wanting it – we need people who genuinely want to do this work,” Krim said.

He refers to dedicated institutes established after independence, where primary and middle school teachers, like himself, trained via a model that combined classroom instruction with direct school placements to meet the gap in Arabic instructors.

The centres operated until the late 1990s, when an economic crunch replaced them with the fewer and more selective Ecoles Normales Superieures.

Most teachers today are university graduates, but lack the practical, classroom-first grounding that the older model provided.

Krim said that school curricula must be designed and entrusted to “a qualified body that includes both linguistic and pedagogical expertise, free from all ideology”.

But journalist and analyst Noureddine Bessadi said the ideological dimension matters in Algeria, which overthrew colonialism following a bloody and bitter struggle against the French.

“Since independence in 1962, every shift in language policy has been fought as much on political as pedagogical grounds,” Bessadi told Al Jazeera.

After independence, Algeria’s Arabisation drive, when French was displaced from government and education, was “part of state building and enforcing Algeria’s identity, centring Arabic and Islam”, Bessadi added.

Tamazight, a non-Semitic language spoken by around a quarter of Algeria’s population, was marginalised until 1995, Bessadi said, shaped by an “ideological perception of unity that prioritised linguistic and cultural harmony”.

Critics argue that the transition from French to English is happening faster than the system can keep up with. For one, it is believed that there are not enough qualified English teachers to make the language reforms work.

But one source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that there are enough teachers to roll out this programme in primary schools and that any shortage could be filled through contractors.

In February, Algeria’s education ministry reportedly recruited about 15,000 English language teachers for primary schools.

Rafik Laceb, a lecturer in English at Mouloud Mammeri University in Tizi Ouzou, is cautiously optimistic about the primary school reform. But he considers the parallel push to teach university subjects in English to be rushed and poorly executed.

“Frankly, and beyond any chauvinism, I believe this decision is positive… I believe there is, today, sufficient supervision and evaluation work from the first experience,” Laceb said, in reference to the previous introduction of English in later primary school years.

The university experiment that began in 2023-2024 produced insufficient contact hours, a lack of genuine assessment of students’ English levels and no tracking of their progress.

Around 50 percent of teaching at Tizi Ouzou University’s English department is by younger contract staff, which brings other challenges.

“A young contract teacher must first master the basic principles of medicine before attempting to teach medical terminology in English,” he said.

Currently, children only begin learning a foreign language in the third year of state primary schools, whereas multiple languages are taught at private schools from kindergarten.

Djamel Merah, whose daughter attended private schools before transferring to public secondary school, studied Arabic, French and English simultaneously from kindergarten level.

Merah welcomes the government’s language reforms at state primary schools, which will provide more children with the opportunity to learn English.

“It addresses a question about the gap in opportunities between children who get multilingual education from the start and those in public schools who don’t get the same chance,” he said.

There also appears to be a more organic response among the public that precedes the government’s promotion of the English language.

Krimo Taleb, a bookseller at the Libre Pensee bookshop in Tizi Ouzou, has seen a growth in English-language book sales, particularly among female readers.

“In my opinion, it has nothing to do with government decisions. The majority of young readers today speak three languages fluently,” he said.

His own daughter, a middle school student, reads fluently in Arabic, English and French.

Colleen Hoover, Ana Huang and J. K. Rowling are some of the best-selling authors at his shop.

“Previously, our bookshops provided for English literature students the works of Shakespeare,” Taleb says. “Today, there is a diverse range of English-language titles aimed at the general public.”

However, French remains Algeria’s most influential foreign language. According to the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), Algeria has approximately 15 million French speakers, nearly a third of its population.

There is not a single newspaper published in English and written English by Algerians remains in its infancy.

But there are signs that former colonies are turning their backs on France’s linguistic legacy, particularly in Africa, where Paris’s military and political presence made a resurgence in recent decades .

In March 2025, Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF, accusing it of being a political instrument of Paris.

“Mali made its national languages official in 2023, demoting French to a working language. Burkina Faso followed the same year and Niger in 2025,” Bessadi added. “Even Senegal, which has not removed French as an official language, has begun encouraging local languages at its expense.”

For Krim, Algeria’s linguistic ambitions are not far-fetched, but for it to work, the country needs the “necessary resources… and transparency”.
paragraphs: Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language.
English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence.

On July 25 , Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027.
French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools.
From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French.
“It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera.
It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools.
Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English.

The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets. Road signs are beginning to feature English alongside Arabic, while government ministers’ websites will also have English as an option.
The shift from French to English as Algeria’s secondary language is both sweeping and structural.
It comes amid the most serious diplomatic crisis between the two countries since Algeria’s independence from France in 1962.
In July 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron publicly backed Morocco’s sovereignty claim over Western Sahara.
Algeria, which supports the Sahrawi Polisario Front and hosts over 170,000 Sahrawi refugees, viewed that as highly provocative.
That, and other issues, saw Algeria expel French diplomats , and vice versa.
Algeria’s replacement of French as the country’s second language accelerated after the diplomatic crisis grew.
A rethink of the whole education system in Algeria may be needed.

“First and foremost, specialised training centres must be restored and candidates must not be forced into the teaching profession without wanting it – we need people who genuinely want to do this work,” Krim said.

He refers to dedicated institutes established after independence, where primary and middle school teachers, like himself, trained via a model that combined classroom instruction with direct school placements to meet the gap in Arabic instructors.
The centres operated until the late 1990s, when an economic crunch replaced them with the fewer and more selective Ecoles Normales Superieures.
Most teachers today are university graduates, but lack the practical, classroom-first grounding that the older model provided.
Krim said that school curricula must be designed and entrusted to “a qualified body that includes both linguistic and pedagogical expertise, free from all ideology”.
But journalist and analyst Noureddine Bessadi said the ideological dimension matters in Algeria, which overthrew colonialism following a bloody and bitter struggle against the French.
“Since independence in 1962, every shift in language policy has been fought as much on political as pedagogical grounds,” Bessadi told Al Jazeera.

After independence, Algeria’s Arabisation drive, when French was displaced from government and education, was “part of state building and enforcing Algeria’s identity, centring Arabic and Islam”, Bessadi added.

Tamazight, a non-Semitic language spoken by around a quarter of Algeria’s population, was marginalised until 1995, Bessadi said, shaped by an “ideological perception of unity that prioritised linguistic and cultural harmony”.

Critics argue that the transition from French to English is happening faster than the system can keep up with. For one, it is believed that there are not enough qualified English teachers to make the language reforms work.
But one source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that there are enough teachers to roll out this programme in primary schools and that any shortage could be filled through contractors.
In February, Algeria’s education ministry reportedly recruited about 15,000 English language teachers for primary schools.

Rafik Laceb, a lecturer in English at Mouloud Mammeri University in Tizi Ouzou, is cautiously optimistic about the primary school reform. But he considers the parallel push to teach university subjects in English to be rushed and poorly executed.

“Frankly, and beyond any chauvinism, I believe this decision is positive… I believe there is, today, sufficient supervision and evaluation work from the first experience,” Laceb said, in reference to the previous introduction of English in later primary school years.
The university experiment that began in 2023-2024 produced insufficient contact hours, a lack of genuine assessment of students’ English levels and no tracking of their progress.
Around 50 percent of teaching at Tizi Ouzou University’s English department is by younger contract staff, which brings other challenges.
“A young contract teacher must first master the basic principles of medicine before attempting to teach medical terminology in English,” he said.
Currently, children only begin learning a foreign language in the third year of state primary schools, whereas multiple languages are taught at private schools from kindergarten.
Djamel Merah, whose daughter attended private schools before transferring to public secondary school, studied Arabic, French and English simultaneously from kindergarten level.
Merah welcomes the government’s language reforms at state primary schools, which will provide more children with the opportunity to learn English.
“It addresses a question about the gap in opportunities between children who get multilingual education from the start and those in public schools who don’t get the same chance,” he said.
There also appears to be a more organic response among the public that precedes the government’s promotion of the English language.
Krimo Taleb, a bookseller at the Libre Pensee bookshop in Tizi Ouzou, has seen a growth in English-language book sales, particularly among female readers.
“In my opinion, it has nothing to do with government decisions. The majority of young readers today speak three languages fluently,” he said.
His own daughter, a middle school student, reads fluently in Arabic, English and French.
Colleen Hoover, Ana Huang and J. K. Rowling are some of the best-selling authors at his shop.
“Previously, our bookshops provided for English literature students the works of Shakespeare,” Taleb says. “Today, there is a diverse range of English-language titles aimed at the general public.”

However, French remains Algeria’s most influential foreign language. According to the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), Algeria has approximately 15 million French speakers, nearly a third of its population.
There is not a single newspaper published in English and written English by Algerians remains in its infancy.

In March 2025, Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF, accusing it of being a political instrument of Paris.

For Krim, Algeria’s linguistic ambitions are not far-fetched, but for it to work, the country needs the “necessary resources… and transparency”.

articles.title: Why Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in West Bank are pogroms
articles.summary: Waves of settler attacks, aided by Israel’s military, increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom.
articles.body:
Attacks on Palestinian communities by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, which are often supported by Israeli forces, have gathered pace over the past month since settlers from the Havat Gilad settlement attacked Palestinian homes on the eastern edge of Tal, southwest of Nablus.

On Sunday and Monday, the Israeli military raided multiple towns, villages and refugee camps across the occupied territory, and reports of arrests, home searches and settler attacks have continued to mount.

A 15-day siege on three families comprising 15 people, including two children, in the village of Qusra, which is ongoing, drew a rare public condemnation this month from the United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and its West Bank settlements.

Israel is also pushing ahead with plans for the so-called E1 settlement expansion close to Jerusalem, which human rights organisations warn would essentially sever the West Bank in two, further hampering the freedom of movement of Palestinians on either side of it and endangering the possibility of a Palestinian state.

The West Bank attacks increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom, experts said. United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese described these Israeli attacks against Palestinians as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”.

So why are experts calling settler attacks pogroms, and do they fit the formal definition of one?

Settlers, frequently supported by the Israeli military, have been attacking Palestinian homes, businesses and farmland across the West Bank. Such attacks have been commonplace for decades as settlements have expanded across the territory, but they have gathered pace after October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza. The attacks in the West Bank have become particularly violent and frequent over the past month.

Israeli settlements and outposts across the West Bank are illegal under international law.

According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli settlers now number roughly 780,000 across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They live in 192 settlements and 400 outposts, making up 71 percent of Area C in the West Bank, which is under full Israeli civil and military control, and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley, the commission said.

Settlers often set up outposts without formal approval around Palestinian villages from which they launch a campaign of harassment, including killing and stealing livestock; cutting off water, electricity and supplies; and damaging property to drive local residents out. Once they establish a more formal settlement, they often receive retrospective approval from the Israeli government for the settlement.

In some places more recently, settlers have laid siege to individual family homes, such as in the Ras al-Ein area of Qusra , cutting off water and other supplies and damaging orchards or harming livestock.

This has set a new pattern: Settlers establish a tent adjacent to individual homes; Palestinians’ homes are besieged with essentials cut off; and Israeli soldiers arrive, not to remove the settlers but rather to remove the family – through arrests or for their “protection”.

In Qusra, the three besieged families were forced together into one of the family houses. Meanwhile, Israeli forces have occupied one of the other homes for use as a military post and thrown furniture and belongings from its windows, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day and marking the fastest pace since the agency began systematic tracking two decades ago.

Separately, a UN-appointed commission of inquiry has found that the Israeli authorities have repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and, in some cases, have directly enabled them through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding.

OCHA has found that settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forcibly displaced more Palestinians in the first four months of this year than in the whole of 2025.

OCHA reported that 107 communities, comprising 5,900 Palestinians, had been completely or partially displaced as a result of settler violence since January 2023. It also found that the Israeli military has expelled another 32,000 Palestinians from their homes in the West Bank since January 2025, essentially emptying the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.

Major dictionaries in the US and United Kingdom vary to some degree on the definition.

The British Collins Dictionary identifies a pogrom as “organised, official violence against a group of people for racial or religious reasons” with a notable inclusion of official, or state-backed, violence.

The Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary calls it “the organised killing of large numbers of people, because of their race or religion” without mention of state-sanctioned violence.

Merriam-Webster says it is “an organised massacre of helpless people” – “specifically: such as a massacre of Jews”.

Cambridge Dictionary says it is “an act of organised cruel behaviour or killing that is done to a large group of people because of their race or religion”.

The word is understood to have been introduced via Yiddish and was at first used to describe the wave of violent, organised mob attacks on Jewish communities in the Russian Empire after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881.

It is important to note that unlike legal terms, including “crimes against humanity” or “genocide”, “pogrom” has no established legal definition under international law.

Can attacks in the West Bank be referred to as pogroms?

Besides UN Special Rapporteur Albanese, who has described Israeli attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”, Israeli officials themselves have described such attacks as “pogroms”.

On February 26, 2023, hundreds of Israeli settlers attacked Huwara and surrounding Palestinian communities after two Israeli settlers were killed. A Palestinian was killed, hundreds were injured, and homes, businesses and cars were burned.

The Israeli military’s then-commander in the West Bank, Yehuda Fuchs, called the settler attacks a “pogrom”, and it was also recorded as such by the US Department of State .

The Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem has also previously described Israeli actions in the West Bank as “pogroms”, especially after the February 2023 attacks. Later, it followed up with a report titled, The Pogroms Are Working – the Transfer Is Already Happening, which argued that settler attacks were contributing to the displacement of Palestinian communities.

“Settler violence is not a new phenomenon, but over the past three years, it has become more violent, more systematic and, most importantly, part of a state mechanism intended to ethnically cleanse large parts of the West Bank,” said Yair Dvir, the spokesperson for B’Tselem.

“The government funds and arms the settlers while the Israeli military stands by and, in many cases, actively participates in the attacks,” he told Al Jazeera. “So far, these militias have expelled 64 Palestinian communities and taken control of around 1 million dunams [100,000 hectares/247,100 acres] of land.”

Dvir also told Al Jazeera that the Israeli settlers are “now carrying out organised attacks on established Palestinian villages and towns in order to drive out their residents”.

“These are armed militias operating as an unofficial arm of the state with a shared goal: to ethnically cleanse as much of the West Bank as possible,” he added.

The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention – which is named after Polish Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who is credited with coining the term genocide after the Holocaust – referred to settler attacks on al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village in the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorate, as “pogroms”, reporting that hundreds of armed settlers attacked residents and burned buildings and cars while soldiers stood by this year. In 2025, the Israeli military uprooted thousands of Palestinian olive trees in al-Mughayyir.

Raheel Dhattiwala, an Indian scholar who focuses on collective violence, told Al Jazeera: “West Bank attacks fit the characteristics of a pogrom – systematic targeting of one civilian group by another with state approval. A few senior Israeli army officers have called it ‘pogroms’ in the past too, for example after attacks in Huwara.

“One might want to debate the use of the term ‘pogrom’, but it is accurate to call settler violence systematic attacks of occupiers with government approval on groups of occupied people.”

articles.title: Japan lawmakers visit China seeking to ease tensions over Taiwan
articles.summary: A cross-party delegation lands in Beijing as Tokyo tries to defrost its worst China rift in decades.
articles.body:
Japanese lawmakers have travelled to Beijing in a bid to soothe strained relations between the two nations.

The delegation landed in China on Monday for talks aimed at restoring communication. The mission was undertaken after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi issued comments on Taiwan that triggered a diplomatic dispute that has begun to weigh on economic relations.

list 1 of 3 Japan’s economy slows, missing growth forecasts

list 2 of 3 Japanese minister visits shrine to war dead, angering China, South Korea

list 3 of 3 US accuses dozens of countries of helping China avoid Trump’s tariffs

The visit will run through Thursday and marks the first such consultations with senior Chinese Communist Party officials since ties soured late last year.

Relations plunged after Takaichi suggested in November that Japan could respond militarily if China attacked Taiwan, a self-governing island that Beijing claims as its own territory.

China is highly sensitive regarding Taiwan and considers questioning of its claim on the island a red line. In response to Takaichi’s comments, it warned its citizens against travel to Japan and tightened trade restrictions, including measures that reportedly disrupted the flow of rare earth minerals to Japanese firms, adding an economic sting to the diplomatic fallout.

Among those making the trip was Gaku Hashimoto, a member of the House of Representatives and Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party. He was joined by other lawmakers from the opposition Komeito and Centrist Reform Alliance parties.

An official from Hashimoto’s office confirmed only that he had “departed for Beijing to stay for two days”.

Before leaving Tokyo, delegation member Shinichi Isa, a spokesperson for the Centrist Reform Alliance, told reporters: “Communication has been severed in all areas, and we are beginning to see their impact in many areas. I hope we can somehow find a clue to restart a dialogue.”

Isa, a former diplomat at the Japanese embassy in China, had already sounded the alarm over the situation this month in a post on X, writing that officials had always managed to stay in contact even during past low points but now “all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”

He described the current state of relations as the worst since diplomatic ties were normalised in 1972.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that “some people of insight from both Japan’s ruling and opposition parties” were troubled by the state of relations and hoped to help steer them back on track while calling on Tokyo to heed those voices and act to restore normal exchanges between the two countries.

Takaichi has not retracted her comment on Taiwan and is yet to respond to the concerns.

Further exchanges are planned. Former Japanese Foreign Minister Takeshi Iwaya is expected to lead another delegation to China in late September, which is to be followed by a group of Japanese business representatives later in the year, according to the Kyodo News agency.

articles.title: Kidnappers release video showing hundreds abducted from Nigerian mosque
articles.summary: Mass kidnappings highlight Nigeria’s security crisis in the north as elections approach.
articles.body:
Kidnappers have released a video of what appears to be a large group of people being held captive by armed men in a forested area in Nigeria.

The video emerged on Sunday, two days after gunmen abducted as many as 600 worshippers during Friday prayers at a mosque in Dekera village in Nigeria’s north-central Niger state.

list 1 of 3 Armed men kidnap dozens in attacks on Nigerian villages

list 2 of 3 Nigeria announces rescue of 308 kidnapped citizens

list 3 of 3 Dozens of abducted schoolchildren and teachers rescued in Nigeria

The incident comes as Nigeria prepares for presidential elections in January, with security likely to be high on the agenda due to a wave of mass kidnappings for ransom across the north of the country.

Dekera village residents have reported that gunmen took people away in simultaneous raids on several communities.

In the video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp and circulating widely, children can be heard crying. A gunman speaking in the Hausa language speaks directly to families of the captives, telling them to identify relatives.

“These are all your people,” the gunman ⁠says.

News agencies reported that they could not verify the exact date or location where the video was filmed. However, no older version of the video has been found posted online before Sunday.

Residents, including Abdulmutallib Muqaddas Dindi, were able to confirm the identities of some ⁠of the hostages.

“We have identified our elders, relatives, and some of us have seen their wives and children in the video,” he said.

Police and state authorities have not responded to requests for comment.

Amnesty International has urged Nigerian authorities to secure the release of the worshippers, warning of the growing threat posed by mass abductions in northern Nigeria.

State Commissioner for Information and Orientation Obed Nana told the Anadolu news agency that an operation is under way to “assess the situation, track the attackers, and facilitate the rescue of the abducted worshippers”.

Mass abductions for ransom have become common in parts of northwestern and north-central Nigeria, with armed gangs frequently raiding villages, schools and highways and holding abductees until the gangs are paid large sums of money.

Increasingly, the gunmen are targeting communities further south, beyond ‌hot spots in the north.

As he prepares for the election, President Bola Tinubu has faced growing criticism over lax security.
