articles.title: Why Trump is escalating his trade war with Canada — and what it means for you
articles.summary: Both sides have announced new 50% tariffs that could make everyday goods more expensive. Trump has also threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lak...
articles.body:
Canada on Tuesday announced new retaliatory tariffs as high as 50% on more than 700 U.S. goods, including steel, clothing, appliances, tools and fish. The new measures, which go into effect on Sept. 8, come after trade talks between the two countries collapsed over the weekend, sparking a full-blown trade war.

On Monday, two days after following through on an earlier tariff threat, President Trump threatened to increase tariffs on all cars, trucks, car parts and steel from Canada to 50% starting next year. Trump also said he's " giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America ."

Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social that Canada was "among the worst Nations in the World to deal" with and warned that America's northern neighbor " will be treated like a State no longer ."

"The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada," the president said in a subsequent post . "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!"

Trump's remarks — and Canada's response — followed weeks of negotiations and frequent claims from Trump that a deal was close. Both sides announced late Friday that they had failed to come to terms. At midnight on Saturday, the Trump administration followed through on its earlier threat to impose new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods, including hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits, wine, cement, honey, makeup, perfume, jewelry, furniture and cameras.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared on Saturday that Canada was now "at war" with the U.S. over the tariffs, vowing a "dollar for dollar" response.

"We learned from the U.S. team during negotiations that [Trump] wants to destroy our major industries," Carney told reporters on Monday. "That's one of the major reasons that led us to say 'no.' It was a bad deal."

Can U.S.-Canada relations be repaired? If not, how will all of these new tariffs affect you? Trump has been trying to transform America's alliance with one of its biggest trading partners since returning to office in January 2025. Here's where things stand right now — and what could come next.

The U.S. and Canada have been conducting on-again, off-again trade talks since the start of Trump's second term. The latest round began in late July after Trump threatened to impose new 50% import taxes in response to Canada's retaliatory measures against his earlier waves of tariffs. The goal was to deescalate the dispute and reach some sort of lasting deal.

As recently as last week , leaders from both countries were saying that a deal was effectively done. The full details of the proposed agreement were never released, but the broad framework would have included Trump dropping his threat to impose the new 50% tariffs in exchange for removing what the U.S. views as unfair barriers to trade — particularly when it comes to agriculture and energy.

Another topic that was discussed was the revival of Keystone XL, a pipeline that was intended to carry large amounts of Canadian oil into the United States before the project was shuttered by former President Joe Biden. On Aug. 18, Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. and Canada had reached a deal and suggested that the pipeline could be "awoken from the grave."

The deal fell apart, however, after Canadian leaders said that the U.S. was trying to assert more control over their country's economy than it was willing to surrender.

"Last minute changes in the U.S. proposed deal were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney wrote in a social media post Friday night in which he announced that he was formally suspending trade talks.

One of the big sticking points , Carney said, was American demands that amounted to "threats on the French language," which he said would "never be acceptable" in Canada's bilingual economy. Trump denied that language issues were ever part of the trade talks, saying, "This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister."

The breakdown of negotiations has sparked a renewed wave of threats and insults that appeared to be pushing the two countries even further apart.

Carney said Monday that Canada won't be returning to the negotiating table until he's confident the U.S. will approach any new talks with "the right attitude" and won't treat his country as a "subsidiary of the United States."

Doug Ford, the premier of the Canadian province of Ontario, was much less diplomatic. Standing in front of a sign that read "Protect Ontario" and flanked by construction workers on Monday, Ford urged Canada to inflict "massive pain" on the U.S. in retaliation for Trump's tariffs. He also took personal shots at the president, calling him a "loser" and telling Trump to "kiss my ass."

"He underestimates Canada. We're all in," Ford told the Associated Press . "Up here, we're at a fever pitch, everyone's in for an economic war."

Trump attacked Ford in kind in a post on Truth Social Monday, calling him a "flunky" and describing him as a "less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive" alternative to his late brother Rob Ford — who was mayor of Toronto from 2010 to 2014.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday suggested Canada was refusing to " negotiate in good faith " throughout the trade talks. He also suggested that Carney's choice to take a firm stance in trade talks was rooted more in his own political interests than the economic interests of the Canadian people.

"Unfortunately, Prime Minister Carney rose to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump platform. … He seems to have gone back to his old playbook," Bessent said.

Bessent's Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told reporters Monday that his country can only tolerate so much from the U.S. before it is forced to punch back.

"At some stage you have to say enough is enough," he said. "We stood up for our economic sovereignty. … We're gonna be the master of our own destiny."

How the U.S.-Canada trade war could affect you

On Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that "there's no possible way" new tariffs "can really affect U.S. well-being."

But economists note that a tariff is an import tax paid by the company doing the importing — not by the foreign country (or foreign business) sending its goods to the U.S. The same experts have found that importers often pass at least some of the added cost of tariffs on to U.S. consumers through higher prices, rather than replacing the affected goods with American-made alternatives.

So it stands to reason that Trump's new 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods — hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits and so on — could make those products more expensive for Americans.

At the same time, U.S. businesses can suffer if they have to pay more for imported Canadian parts or raw materials, or if their products suddenly cost more in Canada because of retaliatory tariffs. Already, U.S. automakers have cut back production north of the border because of tariffs on steel and auto parts, which also raise repair and insurance costs. Meanwhile, Trump has complained that Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars have plummeted since last spring.

Canada's new retaliatory tariffs could have a similar effect on U.S. steel, clothing, fish, tools, appliances and other affected items.

On Monday, Ford also threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. The Pentagon increasingly relies on the latter for use in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics. (For geopolitical reasons, it is always seeking sources other than China.) As for electricity, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on power exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York during an earlier phase of the U.S.-Canada dispute — then retreated when Trump threatened to double steel and aluminum tariffs.

But this time around, Ford insisted that "everything's on the table."

"We power 1.5 million [U.S.] homes and businesses," he said. "I'll do whatever it takes."

For the last 150 years , U.S. presidents have largely maintained close, cordial relations with America's " nicer " neighbors to the north. Trump, in contrast, spent the first weeks of his second term threatening to turn Canada into "the 51st state " and publicly referring to the country's then-prime minister and Liberal Party leader, Justin Trudeau, as "Governor" Trudeau .

In February 2025, Trump imposed sweeping 25% tariffs on goods from both Canada and Mexico. He later increased the tariff on many Canadian exports to 35% while imposing individual tariffs on steel, auto parts and other major industries.

Some have speculated that Trump's animosity toward Canada is rooted in his troubled business dealings there, including a Toronto hotel and condominium complex that went into receivership in 2016 and a Vancouver hotel that filed for bankruptcy and closed in 2020 . Others have noted Trump's fractious relationship with the progressive Trudeau, 54, who was famously photographed greeting first lady Melania Trump with a European cheek kiss at a 2019 Group of 7 gathering in France. A few months later, Trump called his Canadian counterpart "two-faced " for appearing to mock him at a meeting of NATO leaders. The previous year, Trump accused Trudeau of being "very dishonest and weak."

But the simpler explanation for Trump's aggressive trade stance is that the president might see Canada less as the United States' closest ally and more as yet another country that, in his view, has been freeloading and ripping America off — and he's determined to leverage Washington's vast economic power over Ottawa to renegotiate any existing deals on more favorable "America First" terms.

"It's not fair for us to be supporting Canada," Trump said at a Cabinet meeting in February 2025 . "If we don't support them, they don't subsist as a nation."

This is not a new theme for Trump. During his first term, he railed against the steep tariffs Canada imposes on U.S. dairy imports to protect its own domestic farmers, calling them a " disgrace ." In 2018, he slapped 25% tariffs on Canadian steel and 10% tariffs on Canadian aluminum — a move that resulted in at least 75,000 job losses across the U.S. manufacturing sector by mid-2019, according to economists .

Likewise, Trump has long complained that the modest U.S. trade deficit with Canada amounts to a "subsidy," even though experts say it mostly exists because the U.S. imports a lot of inexpensive Canadian oil, which helps lower Americans' gas prices . And Trump also disapproved of Canada spending less than 2% of its GDP on defense — a gripe he had with European NATO member nations as well. (Canada and others have since stepped up their spending .)

As a result, Trump has spent much of his second term escalating the economic pressure on Canada — imposing tariffs; stacking those tariffs with additional duties on steel and aluminum ; picking a trade fight over Canadian lumber ; withdrawing from earlier trade talks over a "fake" Ronald Reagan ad — in an apparent effort to use the United States' economic leverage over Canada to secure more favorable terms at the negotiating table.

Now, that campaign seems to have ruptured U.S.-Canada relations. Canadian sentiment toward the U.S. soured as soon as Trump started his "51st state" insults, according to the New York Times , with some Canadians boycotting American goods and canceling their U.S. vacations . The Canadian government imposed retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars of American exports; some provinces went so far as to pull certain U.S. products from their shelves. Trudeau's Liberal Party, which had been suffering in the polls, rebounded ahead of Carney taking over as prime minister in March and won last April's federal election. Since then, Carney has repeatedly said that Canada's old relationship with America is over.
paragraphs: Canada on Tuesday announced new retaliatory tariffs as high as 50% on more than 700 U.S. goods, including steel, clothing, appliances, tools and fish. The new measures, which go into effect on Sept. 8, come after trade talks between the two countries collapsed over the weekend, sparking a full-blown trade war.

On Monday, two days after following through on an earlier tariff threat, President Trump threatened to increase tariffs on all cars, trucks, car parts and steel from Canada to 50% starting next year. Trump also said he's " giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America ."
Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social that Canada was "among the worst Nations in the World to deal" with and warned that America's northern neighbor " will be treated like a State no longer ."

"The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada," the president said in a subsequent post . "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!"

Trump's remarks — and Canada's response — followed weeks of negotiations and frequent claims from Trump that a deal was close. Both sides announced late Friday that they had failed to come to terms. At midnight on Saturday, the Trump administration followed through on its earlier threat to impose new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods, including hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits, wine, cement, honey, makeup, perfume, jewelry, furniture and cameras.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared on Saturday that Canada was now "at war" with the U.S. over the tariffs, vowing a "dollar for dollar" response.

"We learned from the U.S. team during negotiations that [Trump] wants to destroy our major industries," Carney told reporters on Monday. "That's one of the major reasons that led us to say 'no.' It was a bad deal."

Can U.S.-Canada relations be repaired? If not, how will all of these new tariffs affect you? Trump has been trying to transform America's alliance with one of its biggest trading partners since returning to office in January 2025. Here's where things stand right now — and what could come next.

The U.S. and Canada have been conducting on-again, off-again trade talks since the start of Trump's second term. The latest round began in late July after Trump threatened to impose new 50% import taxes in response to Canada's retaliatory measures against his earlier waves of tariffs. The goal was to deescalate the dispute and reach some sort of lasting deal.

As recently as last week , leaders from both countries were saying that a deal was effectively done. The full details of the proposed agreement were never released, but the broad framework would have included Trump dropping his threat to impose the new 50% tariffs in exchange for removing what the U.S. views as unfair barriers to trade — particularly when it comes to agriculture and energy.

Another topic that was discussed was the revival of Keystone XL, a pipeline that was intended to carry large amounts of Canadian oil into the United States before the project was shuttered by former President Joe Biden. On Aug. 18, Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. and Canada had reached a deal and suggested that the pipeline could be "awoken from the grave."
The deal fell apart, however, after Canadian leaders said that the U.S. was trying to assert more control over their country's economy than it was willing to surrender.

"Last minute changes in the U.S. proposed deal were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney wrote in a social media post Friday night in which he announced that he was formally suspending trade talks.

One of the big sticking points , Carney said, was American demands that amounted to "threats on the French language," which he said would "never be acceptable" in Canada's bilingual economy. Trump denied that language issues were ever part of the trade talks, saying, "This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister."
The breakdown of negotiations has sparked a renewed wave of threats and insults that appeared to be pushing the two countries even further apart.

Carney said Monday that Canada won't be returning to the negotiating table until he's confident the U.S. will approach any new talks with "the right attitude" and won't treat his country as a "subsidiary of the United States."

Doug Ford, the premier of the Canadian province of Ontario, was much less diplomatic. Standing in front of a sign that read "Protect Ontario" and flanked by construction workers on Monday, Ford urged Canada to inflict "massive pain" on the U.S. in retaliation for Trump's tariffs. He also took personal shots at the president, calling him a "loser" and telling Trump to "kiss my ass."
"He underestimates Canada. We're all in," Ford told the Associated Press . "Up here, we're at a fever pitch, everyone's in for an economic war."

Trump attacked Ford in kind in a post on Truth Social Monday, calling him a "flunky" and describing him as a "less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive" alternative to his late brother Rob Ford — who was mayor of Toronto from 2010 to 2014.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday suggested Canada was refusing to " negotiate in good faith " throughout the trade talks. He also suggested that Carney's choice to take a firm stance in trade talks was rooted more in his own political interests than the economic interests of the Canadian people.
"Unfortunately, Prime Minister Carney rose to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump platform. … He seems to have gone back to his old playbook," Bessent said.
Bessent's Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told reporters Monday that his country can only tolerate so much from the U.S. before it is forced to punch back.
"At some stage you have to say enough is enough," he said. "We stood up for our economic sovereignty. … We're gonna be the master of our own destiny."
How the U.S.-Canada trade war could affect you
On Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that "there's no possible way" new tariffs "can really affect U.S. well-being."

But economists note that a tariff is an import tax paid by the company doing the importing — not by the foreign country (or foreign business) sending its goods to the U.S. The same experts have found that importers often pass at least some of the added cost of tariffs on to U.S. consumers through higher prices, rather than replacing the affected goods with American-made alternatives.
So it stands to reason that Trump's new 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods — hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits and so on — could make those products more expensive for Americans.

At the same time, U.S. businesses can suffer if they have to pay more for imported Canadian parts or raw materials, or if their products suddenly cost more in Canada because of retaliatory tariffs. Already, U.S. automakers have cut back production north of the border because of tariffs on steel and auto parts, which also raise repair and insurance costs. Meanwhile, Trump has complained that Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars have plummeted since last spring.
Canada's new retaliatory tariffs could have a similar effect on U.S. steel, clothing, fish, tools, appliances and other affected items.

On Monday, Ford also threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. The Pentagon increasingly relies on the latter for use in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics. (For geopolitical reasons, it is always seeking sources other than China.) As for electricity, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on power exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York during an earlier phase of the U.S.-Canada dispute — then retreated when Trump threatened to double steel and aluminum tariffs.
But this time around, Ford insisted that "everything's on the table."
"We power 1.5 million [U.S.] homes and businesses," he said. "I'll do whatever it takes."

articles.title: Kurdish-led forces in Syria dissolve after merging with army
articles.summary: Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) commander campaigns for Kurdish language preservation after decade fighting ISIL.
articles.body:
The head of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which spearheaded the fight in Syria against the ISIL (ISIS) armed group, has announced its dissolution as part of a deal struck with the government in Damascus.

“We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and declare, with full responsibility, their dissolution as an independent military force,” Mazloum Abdi said on Tuesday evening in a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus.

list 3 of 4 Syria ‘shakes off’ past with removal from US ‘terror’ list, says al-Sharaa

list 4 of 4 Syria’s economy poised for improvement after US sanctions removal

The SDF once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria’s northeast. Abdi said the group has completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force.

The Kurdish-led force lost most of its territory in northeastern Syria in January during a government offensive and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

The SDF was once the main partner of the United States in Syria as it battled ISIL. But after the ouster of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Washington formed close ties with the new government in Damascus, led by interim Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the leader of the opposition forces that overthrew al-Assad.

“Today we stand at a historic moment in which we turn an important page in Syria’s history and begin to open a new page titled peace, stability and reconstruction,” Abdi was quoted as saying by the state news agency, SANA.

“We want this day to be the beginning of a true transition from the battlefields to the fields of construction and from the era of weapons to the era of peace,” he added.

On a cultural note, Abdi said al-Sharaa has recognised the “preservation of our right to education in the Kurdish language”, adding that they would work to implement “education in the Kurdish language during the current year”.

“We want to build a new Syria for all its people – the Kurds, Arabs, Turkmen and Assyrians – a unified and stable Syria that protects the future of its children and ensures a dignified life for its youth,” he said, according to SANA.

United States Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, lauded President Trump’s “far-sighted leadership [that] opened the path for the SDF’s orderly integration into Syrian state institutions.”

“Recognizing the Kurdish language in education and securing substantive roles for our valued partners Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmed within the Syrian government pays due respect to their leadership, the sacrifices of our Kurdish partners, and the constructive contribution they have made to regional stability—turning yesterday’s separations into tomorrow’s shared purpose,” Barrack wrote in a post on X.

Abdi’s announcement came a day after the US removed Syria from its “state sponsors of terrorism” list, a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions. It marked another step in closer ties between the two countries after the ouster of al-Assad.

Al-Sharaa hailed the move, saying, “Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding.”

articles.title: Second man charged with murder after house fire
articles.summary: Slawomir Alama is accused of one count of murder and eight of attempted murder.
articles.body:
A second man has been charged with murder following a fatal house fire in west London last week, the Metropolitan Police have said.

Emergency services were called to the property on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow at about 01:15 BST on 19 August following reports of a fire. Nine people were taken to hospital.

Anna Kowalska, 50, died in hospital, and a 40-year-old woman remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The remaining seven people - six men and one woman - have since been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries.

Slawomir Alama, 41, of Bath Road, Hounslow, has been charged with murder and eight counts of attempted murder.

He has also been charged with arson with intent to endanger life, possession of a class B drug, and possession of a knife in a public place.

Alama was arrested on Tuesday in Leeds, the Met said, supported by West Yorkshire Police.

He has been remanded into custody and is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

It follows the charging of Pawel Kulpa, 34, of no fixed address, who appeared on Monday accused of one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder, and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

Kulpa is next due to appear at the Old Bailey on Thursday.

articles.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in US state of Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Experts warn that declining vaccination rates have opened the door for resurgence of disease once largely eradicated.
articles.body:
The US state of Pennsylvania has reported that two residents died from measles , marking the first fatal cases this year of the disease that had previously been largely eradicated in the United States.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Tuesday that both of the deceased were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, but did not share additional details due to privacy concerns.

list 2 of 3 WHO chief says Trump vaccine push goes against ‘decades of evidence’

list 3 of 3 Erica Schwartz confirmed as new CDC chief amid US agency turmoil

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” said Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen.

The US is facing the most severe measles outbreak in years as vaccination rates drop below levels that medical experts say are necessary to confer herd immunity. That decrease has been partly driven by an anti-vaccination movement that includes prominent members of the Trump administration , such as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .

At least 2,777 confirmed cases of measles have been recorded in the US thus far this year. Pennsylvania has been among the hardest hit by the outbreak, recording 393 measles cases across 28 different counties.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order earlier this month calling for the number of recommended vaccines for children to be reduced, continuing a push to roll back decades of scientific consensus on the safety and efficacy of vaccinations .

Trump and Kennedy, also known as RFK Jr, have pushed debunked claims linking vaccinations with autism and purged government health panels tasked with making recommendations on vaccine policy.

“We all thought the Texas outbreak and the deaths there last year would be a wake-up call. Then we had the outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah,” Dr Angela Dunn, former Utah state epidemiologist and previously a division director in infectious disease response at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Reuters news service.

Three people died from a measles outbreak in 2025 that began in West Texas and spread to New Mexico.

articles.title: Trump administration: Kennedy Center may be demolished if repairs not made
articles.summary: Department of Justice lawyers told a federal judge the venue ‘cannot survive’ without the US president’s help.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has warned that Washington, DC’s Kennedy Center could be demolished if renovations are not allowed to be completed.

In a Monday court filing , US Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyers told a federal judge the performing arts venue is in “terrible trouble,” adding that it “cannot survive, either structurally or financially” without the help of the president or his administration.

list 1 of 3 Whistleblower claims Kennedy Center ‘rushed’ renovations to please Trump

list 2 of 3 Kennedy Center board says it won’t try to immediately restore Trump’s name

list 3 of 3 Kennedy Center votes to restore Trump’s name to venue, close for two years

“Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down,” the filing said.

According to the DOJ filing, an outdoor ampitheatre, overlooking the adjacent Potomac River, could be built on the site if the venue is torn down. The lawyers said that replacement – which they noted would “fail to adequately honor” the venue’s namesake, former US President John F Kennedy – would be “simpler and more economical”.

The revelation, which marks the most extreme action mentioned for the venue since Trump took control of it after returning to the White House for a second term in 2025, was contained within the administration’s response to an effort to block his name from being inscribed on the building.

US Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat who sits on the Kennedy Center’s board through her leadership position in Congress, sued after Trump-appointed board members voted 20-3 to add the phrase “restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump” beneath existing signage. Previously, the board renamed the venue after Trump before a judge ordered that his name be removed from the building’s façade.

Any decision to tear down the historic Kennedy Center, which opened in 1971 to honour the fallen president, would likely face stiff pushback from preservation groups and those opposed to Trump’s efforts to make changes at the site.

articles.title: Dolly Parton through the years, in photos: From ‘9 to 5’ secretary to ‘Hannah Montana’ godmother
articles.summary: Until she died Tuesday at age 80, Dolly Parton was the beloved Queen of Country music.
articles.body: Dolly Parton craved the camera. And until she died Tuesday at age 80, the Queen of Country’s life unspooled in photograph after photograph, turning the poor little girl with the angelic voice from eastern Tennessee into one of America’s most beloved — and recognizable — figures. It was country singer Porter Wagoner who first introduced Parton to a wider audience when he invited her in 1967 to appear on his hit TV show. By 1974, Parton was out on her own, and her signature public image — the blond wigs, the cleavage-baring outfits that showed off her hourglass figure — was cast in stone. Soon Hollywood beckoned, and Parton took it by storm, winning a Grammy for her single “Here You Come Again” and appearing in a string of hit movies that eventually earned her a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984. Bubbly and witty, Parton was also a must-book guest on the small screen: She made more than 400 television appearances, performing on variety shows hosted by the likes of Cher and Mac Davis, and charming late-night and daytime hosts ranging from Johnny Carson and his successor, Jay Leno, to Oprah Winfrey and Conan O’Brien. Parton also hosted not one, but two TV variety shows, both called “Dolly,” which millions of Americans tuned in to watch. And in 1989, she even took a turn at hosting “Saturday Night Live,” where, during the opening monologue, the running gag was her cracking jokes while the cameraman was unable to focus on anything but her bosom. Her duets with performers ranging from Elton John and Kenny Rogers to Miley Cyrus spanned the generational divide; she became the rarest of performers — one whose fan base expanded as she grew older. With the acclaim came the awards, the invitations to give commencement speeches, the honorary degrees, the chance to perform before thousands of fans at big-time sports events. But there was a part of Parton’s life she mostly kept hidden from America’s prying eyes, the part she is said to have cherished most — her nearly 59-year marriage to her husband, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025. Dean almost never appeared in public with his famous wife and, as a result, there were very few photos of them together available to the public. And they were fine with that. “I’ve kept [my marriage] very personal and sacred and I try to keep my husband out of the business,” she said in an interview. “That’s not what he chose to do, he just happened to love me and I love him enough to not expose him to it.”

articles.title: US judge blocks Ohio law requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote
articles.summary: The amended law was an attempt by state Republicans to crack down on unproven claims of voting by noncitizens.
articles.body:
A United States federal court has temporarily blocked an Ohio law that required proof of US citizenship from residents who wanted to register to vote while they obtained a driver’s license.

In his ruling on Tuesday, US District Judge Solomon Oliver Jr granted a preliminary injunction against the law, saying it likely violates the US National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) because it requires more information than necessary to determine a resident’s eligibility to vote.

list 2 of 3 Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election security

list 3 of 3 Did China steal 2020 US election data, as Trump claims?

“Election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant’s citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough,” Oliver wrote.

The judge also pointed to a clause in the act that says each US state’s driver’s license application “shall serve as an application for voter registration with respect to election for Federal office unless the applicant fails to sign the voter registration application”.

Oliver said that Ohio must offer applicants the opportunity to register once they’ve submitted their driver’s license application, not after it’s been approved by the state’s Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV).

“To interpret this section of the NVRA otherwise would allow States to make registering to vote at the BMV more onerous, and could result in fewer voter registrations because the opportunity to apply was not proactively offered to otherwise eligible citizens,” Oliver added.

In 1995, Ohio passed a so-called “motor-voter” law that allowed residents the opportunity to register to vote when they applied for a driver’s license

But that law was amended last year by the state’s Republican-controlled legislature in an attempt to crack down on unproven claims, pushed in part by US President Donald Trump, that noncitizens were voting in the state’s election. US law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.

The ruling marks a victory for voting rights advocates like Red Wine & Blue, which sued Ohio’s secretary of state, Frank LaRose, over claims that the law disenfranchised eligible voters and violated the NVRA.

One of the group’s lawyers, Ben Stafford, praised the ruling, calling it “a win for Ohio voters.”

“With the registration deadline just weeks away, eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork that is not required by federal law,” Stafford, an attorney at Elias Law Group, said in a statement.

LaRose said his office disagrees with the decision and will appeal.

articles.title: ‘There will never be another Dolly’: Tributes to Parton pour in across generations
articles.summary: Entertainers and celebrities reflected on Parton’s creative talent, while fans and everyday people recounted how her philanthropic generosity touched their lives.
articles.body: Reflecting the magnitude of her influence and impact, Dolly Parton’s death drew immediate tributes from across industries, genres, generations, places and people. Entertainers, film stars, politicians and everyday people who benefited from her generosity and her enterprises quickly filled social media with their stories of how she improved their lives, how her songs uplifted or taught them, how she made them laugh and how they just loved who she was. The accolades poured in from around the globe, offered up from sources as varied as country music superstars Reba McEntire, Kacey Musgraves and Linda Ronstadt to Khloe Kardashian and the Muppets, as well as singers and other celebrities, including Mick Jagger, Dionne Warwick, Pink, Keke Palmer, Lily Tomlin, Kelly Clarkson, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and fashion designer Donatella Versace. President Donald Trump ordered flags lowered for a week, writing on Truth Social, “There has never been anyone like her, and there never will,” as politicians from both sides of the aisle paid tribute. Former President Bill Clinton wrote on social media that Parton was “one of a kind — a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart. She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from.” McEntire wrote of getting the news that “my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side.” She thanked her for “all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth” and said, “There will never ever be another you.” Some of country music’s royalty sang her praises and were joined by a younger generation of musicians and songwriters who heralded her as an inspiration. “This really hurts,” wrote Musgraves, a multiple Grammy award winner. Parton drew an homage from the “King of Country Music,” George Strait, who said on Facebook: “You’ve had such a huge impact all over the world, @dollyparton. We will all miss you. May God bless the Parton family.” The adoration was not confined to country music. “She was a sweet and kind soul and I’m proud to say I knew her. ... There will never be another Dolly,” said Gene Simmons, bassist and co-founder of the hard rock band Kiss. The Muppets posted a black-and-white photo of Parton with Miss Piggy, saying, “She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off.” Comedian Lily Tomlin, Parton’s longtime friend, wrote, “No words...” followed by a broken heart emoji, alongside a black-and-white photo of the two, side by side with large smiles. In a video reel, Tomlin featured photos of herself with Jane Fonda, who co-starred with them in the 1980s hit “9 to 5.” Parton’s title song for the 1980 movie — which topped the Billboard country chart — played in the background. National Organization for Women President Kim Villanueva said in a statement that Parton “defined feminism,” adding that her role in “9 to 5” emphasized that women in the workplace “deserved to be treated equally and with respect.” “She encouraged women to embrace who they wanted to be and stand up for their values,” Villanueva wrote. Donna Brazile, the former chair of the Democratic National Convention, posted that Parton “spent decades quietly funding band uniforms and instruments at Black high schools across the South — never once putting her name on it. No headlines, no fanfare — just help, given because it was needed.” Meanwhile, Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, Parton’s native state, said the state had lost one of its greatest ambassadors, who represented “the very best of the American dream.” Parton’s music “inspired generations of Americans and her philanthropic work helped provide greater access to education for countless young Tennesseans,” he said. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote on X, “Rest in peace, Dolly Parton — a true legend and a force for good.” Parton’s Dollywood Foundation focused on improving children’s educational success and stemming dropout rates in Tennessee. It gave birth to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which sent books to children around the world. Her work was inspired by her father’s illiteracy. A father who said he’s in Australia posted on X that his young daughter got her first book Monday night from Parton’s Imagination Library. All of his children read it with their mother and laughed and enjoyed it, he said. The Library of Congress posted a photo of Parton, with reading glasses, conducting a story time book reading to children at the library. It described her as a “titan of children’s literacy” and said she donated the 100 millionth book to its collection. Parton helped fund crucial infectious disease research, with Scientific American paying tribute to her for her $1 million donation to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, to help fund an early-stage trial of the Covid vaccine in 2020. She told NBC News that she donated to the vaccine effort because “I just wanted to do good.” She also helped promote Covid vaccinations with a video of her getting the shot and an adjustment to her song “Jolene” to “Vaccine.” The Motion Picture Academy awarded her its Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award last year. Dollywood, Parton’s much-beloved theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, will open Wednesday. “In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — ‘the show must go on,’” the company said in a statement. “Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance and hope.”

articles.title: Nitro Camden meets IShowSpeed after viral clash with mother, gets emotional advice: âFollow your dreams, broâ
articles.summary: US Streamers News: IShowSpeed met Nitro Camden in person and offered him a simple message after the young streamer reportedly lost his place at his motherâs home: keep g.
articles.body: IShowSpeed met Nitro Camden in person and offered him a simple message after the young streamer reportedly lost his place at his motherâs home: keep going and follow his goals. Spilled reported that the meeting came days after Camden became known following a livestream involving his mother, which spread across social media. Speed also connected Camdenâs situation to his own early years as a streamer, when his mother wanted him to focus on school. Camden appeared emotional, while Speed showed he understood how difficult family pressure can feel when someone is trying to build a career online today.IShowSpeed tells Nitro Camden to keep chasing his goalsSpeedâs advice was direct. âFollow your dreams, bro.â He also told Camden, âI was in the same situation as you. Do what you wanna do, bro.â Speed said he could not even watch the viral clip involving Camden because it brought back memories of his own experience.For Camden, hearing that from one of the biggest names in streaming made the meeting emotional. He had been streaming to almost no viewers before the recent incident changed everything. Clips from the family argument spread quickly, and his audience grew in a matter of days.The exact details of Camdenâs family situation have not been fully confirmed. His age, where he is staying now and what he plans to do next have also not been clearly established publicly. That makes it difficult to know how much of his sudden rise will last after the attention around the incident slows down.During the conversation, Speed also told Camden, âI couldnât even watch that clipâ¦ âcause it brought up too much.â The comment showed why the meeting was more personal than a usual creator shoutout. Speed was speaking from an experience he said felt familiar to him.Nitro Camdenâs viral rise brings new attention to his streaming careerCamdenâs rise happened very quickly. Before the family footage circulated, he was a small streamer with almost no audience. A raid from other creators then brought many new viewers to his channel, turning him into a name people across the streaming community were suddenly talking about.Speed could relate to part of that journey. Early in his own career, his mother wanted him to give more attention to school instead of streaming. His streams also included risky stunts, including a well-known incident in which he set off a firework inside his home. Despite those problems, he continued creating content and eventually became one of the internetâs biggest streamers.The comparison, however, has limits. The two situations are not confirmed to be the same, and Camdenâs full family story is still unclear. Speedâs message was mainly about not giving up on a goal when people around you do not support it.For now, Camden has not clearly said whether he plans to continue school, stream full time or take another path. His meeting with Speed gave him encouragement, but what happens next will depend on Camden and the circumstances around him.That sudden change is also why the next few weeks could matter. Camden now has a much larger audience, but a viral moment does not automatically become a lasting streaming career. articles.title: Teen Claims She Had a ‘Bad Day’ Before Fatally Shooting Milwaukee Mother in Road Rage Incident: DA
articles.summary: Mariah Ruiz, 18, has been charged in connection with the killing of Minerva Hernandez-Lopez, 44, after a verbal altercation escalated on Aug. 17
articles.body:
Mariah Ruiz, 18, is accused of shooting her 44-year-old mother, Minerva Hernandez-Lopez, after a road rage argument in Milwaukee, according to a criminal complaint obtained by PEOPLE

Ruiz admitted to the shooting, police say, claiming she had a "bad day" and later wrote an apology to the victim's family

If convicted, Ruiz could face up to 65 years in prison

A Milwaukee teen has been accused of killing a 44-year-old mother in a road rage incident after having a bad day.

Mariah Ruiz, 18, has been charged with first-degree reckless homicide by use of a dangerous weapon, according to online records viewed by PEOPLE on Monday, Aug. 24.

The incident occurred on the afternoon of Aug. 17, when Ruiz is accused of engaging in a verbal altercation with Minerva Hernandez-Lopez that later turned deadly, according to a criminal complaint filed in Milwaukee County Circuit Court and obtained by PEOPLE.

PEOPLE has reached out to an attorney for Ruiz, but did not immediately receive a response.

Ruiz allegedly cut Hernandez-Lopez off while she and a 16-year-old friend were on their way to a grocery store, before the verbal altercation ensued. At some point, Hernandez-Lopez allegedly "flicked [Ruiz] off," Ruiz told investigators, according to the criminal complaint.

Hernandez-Lopez allegedly told Ruiz, "Little girl, you need to drive," the 16-year-old told investigators, according to the complaint.

The witness said Ruiz allegedly replied by threatening to call U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Hernandez-Lopez after the victim yelled at her in Spanish, before the situation intensified, per the complaint. Ruiz also told investigators she "threatened to call ICE on the victim," the complaint reads.

Ruiz is then accused of pulling out a gun and following Hernandez-Lopez after their argument.

Hernandez-Lopez's tan GMC was reportedly seen on video backing into Ruiz's front bumper of her Nissan before Ruiz allegedly opened fire, according to the criminal complaint. Five bullet casings were recovered from the scene, where Hernandez-Lopez was pronounced dead.

"We tried everything we could do to help her," Jesus Ferreira, a witness, told WISN in an on-camera interview. "It's something traumatic [that] I've never seen."

The Milwaukee Medical Examiner's Office completed an autopsy, and said Hernandez-Lopez's cause of death was listed as a gunshot wound to the neck and the manner of death was homicide, according to the complaint.

The teen told authorities that she was having a "bad day" after fighting with her mother, the complaint alleges.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Police say Ruiz admitted to shooting and killing Hernandez-Lopez and wrote a letter of apology to the victim's family.

Ruiz, who turned herself in, "stated that she did not mean to hurt the victim and she is not sure why she did it," according to the complaint. She also told investigators that her 16-year-old friend told her not to shoot at the time of the alleged attack.

If convicted, Ruiz could face 65 years in prison.

A cash bond of $100,000 was set for Ruiz. She is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Friday, Aug. 28.

articles.title: Helicopter rescue crew caught on camera saving 2 climbers trapped along popular California beach cliff
articles.summary: Video shows a CHP helicopter crew hovering above a Big Sur ravine to hoist two climbers stranded 600 feet below the roadway at Hurricane Point.
articles.body: Two climbers in California stranded on a steep Big Sur cliffside Saturday found themselves 600 feet below the roadway with a California Highway Patrol (CHP) helicopter crew their only way out. Video released by the CHP shows the H-70 helicopter hovering above a steep ravine near Hurricane Point as a rescue technician is lowered on a cable to reach the trapped pair. Big Sur Fire requested help from CHP’s Paso Robles Air Unit at about 6:24 p.m., according to the agency. NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS The terrain was so steep that the technician could not safely disconnect from the hoist hook after reaching the first climber. Instead, he secured the climber in a Pelican rescue harness and the two were lifted together to rescue personnel waiting at a staging area. The helicopter then returned to the ravine and carried out the same technical maneuver to bring the second climber to safety. RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION CHP did not release the climbers’ names or explain how they became stranded. Social media users praised the CHP air crew and the rescue teams involved after video of the operation was posted online. "Incredible rescue!! Well done guys!!" one commenter wrote. Another called it an "amazing job by all involved," while another added, "Just incredible, you guys, thanks for what you do!" Both climbers survived the ordeal, authorities said. HIKER AIRLIFTED AFTER TERRIFYING RATTLESNAKE BITE ON REMOTE TRAIL AS INCIDENTS SURGE IN AREA "These high-risk, low-frequency rescues are exactly what CHP Air Operations personnel continuously train for," the agency said. "There is no room for error when operating in steep terrain, under hoist, and in challenging environmental conditions." The cliffside rescue followed two separate Aug. 9 rescue missions for the same H-70 crew. MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION The air unit first hoisted an injured 13-year-old hiker from Pinnacles National Park, working with a Paso Robles Fire Department helicopter rescue technician, CHP said. Later that day, the crew pulled a person who suffered severe injuries in a fall from a waterfall in Big Sur Gorge to safety. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP H-70 then responded to another call in the remote Los Padres National Forest, where a hunter suffering from heat exhaustion and dehydration was brought aboard using a hover step-on maneuver and flown to waiting medics in King City.

articles.title: Report: Former Arizona guard Brandon Williams signs with Warriors
articles.summary: Steve Kerr will have a former Arizona guard under his tutelage this NBA season. Brandon Williams has signed a one-year, $2.6 million contract with the Golden...
articles.body:
Steve Kerr will have a former Arizona guard under his tutelage this NBA season.

Brandon Williams has signed a one-year, $2.6 million contract with the Golden State Warriors , ESPN's Shams Charania reported Tuesday.

Free agent guard Brandon Williams has agreed to a one-year, $2.6 million deal to sign with the Golden State Warriors, agents Derek Lafayette and Curtis Lawrence tell ESPN. Williams averaged 13 points, 3.9 assists and 22.2 minutes per night across 66 games for Dallas last season. pic.twitter.com/VcDytjCDKe — Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) August 25, 2026

Free agent guard Brandon Williams has agreed to a one-year, $2.6 million deal to sign with the Golden State Warriors, agents Derek Lafayette and Curtis Lawrence tell ESPN. Williams averaged 13 points, 3.9 assists and 22.2 minutes per night across 66 games for Dallas last season. pic.twitter.com/VcDytjCDKe

The former Wildcats point guard is coming off a career-best season with Dallas Mavericks in which he averaged 13 points and 3.9 assists in 22 minutes per game. Williams appeared in 66 games with Dallas after spending the previous two seasons on two-way deals.

The 26-year-old debuted with Portland in 2021 after going undrafted out of college. Williams missed his sophomore season at Arizona due to a knee injury and spent the following year preparing for a professional career.

Williams, a Los Angeles native, is heading back to his home state to play for a Warriors franchise that has fallen on hard times in recent years. Williams will compete with De'Anthony Melton for the backup point guard role behind Stephen Curry .

Williams is the third former Wildcat to play under Kerr in Golden State, joining Andre Iguodala and Nico Mannion .

articles.title: How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs
articles.summary: A legendary singer-songwriter, her music covered themes around love, loss, female empowerment and spirituality.
articles.body:
The much-loved US singer-songwriter, actress and philanthropist Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80 , was known as the Queen of Country.

Raised in Tennessee, she rose to fame in the late 1960s with hits that bridged country and pop music.

Her songs covered deeply personal themes around growing up poor, love and loss, as well as female empowerment and spirituality.

Live updates: Dolly Parton, legendary US country singer, dies aged 80

Dolly Parton: The country legend who sang from the heart

Following Parton's death, here is a look back at her life through the lens of six iconic songs.

Let's start with Dolly Parton's own personal favourite, her 1971 acoustic country-folk ditty, Coat of Many Colors , external .

The autobiographical track, taken from the album of the same name, tells the heart-stirring tale of how she grew up poor - as one of 12 siblings - but rich in love.

In her book, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics, Parton described it as a "little story" that covers "a world of things", with teachings about bullying, acceptance, love and good parenting.

The lyrics go: " Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my momma made for me " .

The song has been covered by the likes of Shania Twain and Eva Cassidy, and Rolling Stone magazine put it in second place in its list of Parton's top 50 songs , external .

"Had it been the only song she'd ever written, the expression of overwhelming pride and crushing anguish... would have secured her indelible legacy," the US magazine wrote in 2023.

Coat of Many Colors is also the title of Parton's own children's book, and a 2015 TV movie based on her life - starring Alyvia Alyn Lind as the precocious young singer dreaming of fame.

Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, even made her daughter a new patchwork coat to put on display at the museum inside the Dollywood theme park in her home state of Tennessee.

Parton penned many songs about all different aspects of her relationship with her devoted husband Carl Dean , who ran an asphalt paving business in Nashville.

This included the fear that she might lose him, specifically to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.

We all know her by now, of course, as the infamous Jolene , external .

With its fast fingerstyle minor riff, the song was nominated for a Grammy in 1974 and gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).

It also showed Parton at her most vulnerable, making it all the more relatable.

Instead of shedding tears or vowing revenge, we hear the protagonist in the song begging the mistress who holds the power to relinquish it.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband," Parton told US media in 2008. "And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us - I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

Parton had met Dean outside a laundromat on the first day she arrived in Nashville as an 18-year-old aspiring singer. The pair were married for 60 years, until his death in 2025 .

A notoriously private man, he was "a little embarrassed" when she wrote Jolene, Parton said in a 2023 interview with BBC's The One Show , external , adding that "actually, it wasn't as serious [as it sounds]. I was just jealous 'cause she was a beautiful woman and he was just flirting.

"So it gave me a great idea for a song. There's always a Jolene in somebody's life."

She joked that later in life when she saw her, by now, much older husband snoozing in his chair at home, she thought Jolene "can have him now... where's Jolene when you need her?!"

Jolene is her most popular song, having been streamed more than 913 million times on Spotify. Critics from Rolling Stone to the Guardian , external agree it's her best.

BeyoncÃ© gave it a modern rewrite for her 2024 Cowboy Carter , external album, changing the lyrics from: " I'm begging of you, please, don't take my man " to " I'm warning you, don't come for my man. "

Despite the romantic sounding title, this 1974 song , external is actually the sound of Parton tenderly asking her musical mentor, Porter Wagoner, to let her go and pursue her solo career.

Parton was 21 when she joined Wagoner's variety TV show. They released a string of duets and toured together, leading fans to think they were an item.

But they had a complicated relationship, with Parton later writing in another book, Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, that she felt Wagoner saw her rise as a "threat".

"I was making my way as an artist, and he was already an established one. It was his show, but I was trying to grow in the business and grow as an artist myself."

On the track we hear her sing: " Bittersweet memories / That is all I'm taking with me".

Rough Trade's music blog , external once described it as being "heartwarming in its sentiment, crushing in its delivery."

Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song in 1974, but Parton made the difficult decision to back out of the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.

"I said, 'I can't do that'," she told Howard Stern in 2023. "Of course I cried all night about that."

Parton re-recorded I Will Always Love You in 1982 for her starring role in the musical comedy film, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.

But arguably the most iconic version comes courtesy of Whitney Houston who can be heard booming it out in another film, 1992's The Bodyguard. Her version remains the biggest-selling US single by a female artist.

Parton said she heard the power ballad version for the first time on the radio, and felt so overwhelmed that she had to pull over to avoid crashing her Cadillac.

Whitney Houston took her "little country song" and made it "so much more", she said.

With Parton's newfound professional freedom came a renewed sense of hope, optimism and spirituality - as heard on her 1977 track, Light of a Clean Blue Morning.

She recalled leaving Wagoner's office after their musical split and driving home in a rainstorm, until the clouds parted, giving way to sunlight and an idea for another new song.

Parton - whose earliest performances were in church as a child - referred to it as her "song of deliverance", helping her on the road to stardom.

The lyrics were reworked for the soundtrack to her 1992 romantic comedy film, Straight Talk.

And in early 2026 she released a new charity version of the song , external , in aid of pediatric cancer research, featuring her goddaughter Miley Cyrus, Lainey Wilson, Queen Latifah and Reba.

This defiant anthem of female empowerment, released in 1980, was the most transformative of her career.

Already well established as a singer, 9 To 5 , external brought Parton over into the mainstream popular culture.

She wrote the country-tinged southern soul number as the theme tune for the comedy film of the same name, which saw her make her movie debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.

It tells the story of three working women who live out their fantasies of getting even with, and overthrowing, their company's bigot of a boss (played by Dabney Coleman).

The song's distinctive tapping beat at the start is none other than her acrylic nails: "I always play the nails and I'd come up with little things that I would see on the set, like 'I tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen'â¦ And I thought, 'Wow, that sounds like a typewriter,'" she once explained.

Parton won two Grammys for the chart-topping tune, which was also nominated for an Oscar, and later spawned a Broadway musical and a documentary.

A modern day karaoke classic, Parton recorded this hit with fellow US country star Kenny Rogers , external as the lead single for his 1983 album, Eyes That See in the Dark.

The deep love song sold millions of copies and topped both the country and pop charts at the same time.

It was actually written for them by the Bee Gees, intended as a Motown-inspired duet. The Gibb brothers later recorded their own version and performed it live.

Parton and Rogers' rendition, though, remains one of most popular country-pop duets of all time and a classic of the genre.

Their collaboration was "another thing I'm as proud of as anything I ever did in my musical career," she told Smooth Radio , external 40 years on, in 2023.

She added: "You want to do well and keeping up with the likes of Barry [Gibb] and Kenny [Rogers], but I just figure I'll just always be me and do me and that seems to work."

Down from Dover , external - the heartbreaking 1970 tale of an abandoned mother giving birth to a stillborn child was controversial and Wagoner warned Parton against releasing it

The Bargain Store , external - a moving lyrical account of a lady, experienced in love and loss, comparing herself to a secondhand shop, from 1975

Here You Come Again , external - written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil and released by Parton in 1977, it saw her skillfully pivot to pop/soft rock to great effect on her first big crossover hit

The song's distinctive tapping beat at the start is none other than her acrylic nails: "I always play the nails and I'd come up with little things that I would see on the set, like 'I tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen'â¦ And I thought, 'Wow, that sounds like a typewriter,'" she once explained.
Parton won two Grammys for the chart-topping tune, which was also nominated for an Oscar, and later spawned a Broadway musical and a documentary.
A modern day karaoke classic, Parton recorded this hit with fellow US country star Kenny Rogers , external as the lead single for his 1983 album, Eyes That See in the Dark.
The deep love song sold millions of copies and topped both the country and pop charts at the same time.
It was actually written for them by the Bee Gees, intended as a Motown-inspired duet. The Gibb brothers later recorded their own version and performed it live.
Parton and Rogers' rendition, though, remains one of most popular country-pop duets of all time and a classic of the genre.
Their collaboration was "another thing I'm as proud of as anything I ever did in my musical career," she told Smooth Radio , external 40 years on, in 2023.
She added: "You want to do well and keeping up with the likes of Barry [Gibb] and Kenny [Rogers], but I just figure I'll just always be me and do me and that seems to work."
Down from Dover , external - the heartbreaking 1970 tale of an abandoned mother giving birth to a stillborn child was controversial and Wagoner warned Parton against releasing it
The Bargain Store , external - a moving lyrical account of a lady, experienced in love and loss, comparing herself to a secondhand shop, from 1975
Here You Come Again , external - written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil and released by Parton in 1977, it saw her skillfully pivot to pop/soft rock to great effect on her first big crossover hit

articles.title: BJ’s Wholesale customers will face a significant store change
articles.summary: BJ’s Wholesale is planning a major change as it responds to an evolving shopping environment.
articles.body:
BJ's Wholesale is planning a significant change to its in-store offerings as it sees customer behavior shift.

In the second quarter of this year, the warehouse club saw its comparable club sales (including gasoline) increase by 11.9% year over year, according to the latest earnings report . Its membership also grew to a record 8.5 million.

As sales grew, BJ's overall customer visits rose by 4.9% year over year, slightly outpacing Sam's Club's 4.7% increase, according to recent Placer.ai data . The stronger demand comes as BJ's has been working to offer members lower prices using tariff refunds it received from the government.

"Traditional grocers have been raising prices, creating an even more favorable backdrop for our value proposition," said BJ's Wholesale CEO Bob Eddy on an earnings call on Aug. 21 . "We continue to gain share, and as our price gaps improve, unit share has become an even clearer signal of member preference."

As BJ's sees increased demand, Eddy said the company plans to revamp its in-store assortment by reducing SKUs (stock-keeping units), or individual product varieties.

"We find ourselves over-SKUed," said Eddy. "It has been a longstanding opportunity. We have had efforts to cut SKU count in the past, and I would argue we didn't prosecute that opportunity in the right way. We just cut SKUs, which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back."

He said the company is now in the process of "removing unnecessary choice" from its stores, a change members will gradually notice.

Instead of carrying multiple versions of the same product, BJ's will narrow its selection, concentrate sales among the remaining versions, and add new, innovative items in untapped categories.

Eddy said the company has already made these changes in its beverages and active nutrition categories, which are already yielding positive results.

Related: BJ's Wholesale plans major store changes as customers pull back

"Think about in traditional soda, we do not carry cans and 1-liter and 2-liters of the same product anymore," said Eddy. "We are adding in healthy soda, like Poppi and things like that. That is the idea around the building."

He said these changes will roll out over the next few years, with the next waves happening in September and toward the end of the year.

"Our goal really is to take about 20% of our SKUs out over the next couple of years, and that will sort of happen ratably," said Eddy. "That will largely get the chain down to where we find ourselves in new clubs, maybe a little bit lower than that."

articles.title: Penn State football announces themes for home games
articles.summary: HAPPY VALLEY, Pa. (WHTM) — Penn State football announced themes for its home games this year. The game that draws the most attention, the White Out Game, wil...
articles.body:
HAPPY VALLEY, Pa. (WHTM) -- Penn State football announced themes for its home games this year.

The game that draws the most attention, the White Out Game , will be Oct. 10 when the Nittany Lions take on USC at 7:30 p.m.

For the home opener against Marshall on Sept. 5, the theme is the 11th annual "Stripe Out," where fans are encouraged to wear either white or blue depending on where they will sit.

The THON game this year will be when Penn State plays Buffalo on Sept. 19. Then, when the Nittany Lions take on Wisconsin Sept. 26, that will be the homecoming and helmet stripe game.

The game against Purdue on Oct. 31 will be the ALL-U Day game, then the Nov. 14 game against Minnesota will be the military appreciation game and Senior Day is Nov. 21 when Penn State plays against Rutgers.

Penn State Football fans will get closer than ever to the team this fall with Nittany Nation & Nittany Insiders .
